summary: This Wikipedia article describes the circular flow of income, a model of the economy in which money, goods and services move between economic agents in a closed loop, forming the basis of national accounts and macroeconomics. It traces the concept's history from Richard Cantillon and François Quesnay through Karl Marx, Keynes, Frank Knight and Richard Stone, and explains the two-, three-, four- and five-sector versions of the model. It also covers leakages and injections across the financial, government and overseas sectors. The note is truncated before the equilibrium, significance and environment sections.
one_line: Wikipedia article on the circular flow of income, a model of money and goods moving between economic sectors and its history from Cantillon to Keynes.
key_facts: The circular flow of income is a model of the economy in which major exchanges are represented as flows of money, goods and services between economic agents.
The flows of money and goods exchanged in a closed circuit correspond in value but run in opposite directions.
The circular flow analysis is the basis of national accounts and hence of macroeconomics.
Richard Cantillon's 1730 Essay on the Nature of Trade in General contained an early circular-flow model.
François Quesnay visualized the concept in the Tableau économique, published in 1758.
Quesnay argued that agricultural surpluses, flowing through the economy as rent, wages and purchases, were the real economic movers.
Karl Marx developed Quesnay's insights in the second volume of Das Kapital, modeling the circulation of capital, money and commodities.
John Maynard Keynes published the General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1933.
Frank Knight is described as the first to visualize the modern circular flow of income model, in his 1933 publication The Economic Organization.
Richard Stone further developed the concept for the United Nations and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, and it is now used internationally.
The two-sector model comprises households and firms and assumes no financial, government or foreign sector.
The three-sector model adds the government sector, with flows from households and firms to government in the form of taxes.
The four-sector model adds the foreign sector, also known as the external sector, overseas sector or rest of the world.
The five-sector model adds the financial sector, which includes banks and non-bank intermediaries that borrow savings from households and lend to firms.

Leakages (savings, tax payments, imports) reduce the flow of income, while injections (investment, government spending, exports) increase it; as long as leakages equal injections, the circular flow continues indefinitely.
